name: LTC6957IMS-2#TRPBF
title: LTC6957-1/-2/-3/-4: low phase noise dual-output clock buffer and sine-to-logic converter, LVPECL, LVDS or CMOS outputs, 300 MHz
summary: A clock buffer with two outputs that turns a sine wave or a logic signal of up to 2 VP-P and 300 MHz into clean logic edges with very little added phase noise. Selectable low-pass filtering in the early gain stages cuts noise for slowly slewing inputs such as a 10 MHz sine reference. The four versions differ in output: LVPECL (-1), LVDS (-2), in-phase CMOS (-3) and complementary CMOS (-4). It runs from 3.15 V to 3.45 V, with a separate 2.4 V to 3.45 V output supply on the CMOS versions, and comes in 12-lead MSOP and 3 mm × 3 mm DFN.
key_figures: 45 fsRMS typ (LTC6957-1, 12 kHz to 20 MHz, 300 MHz)

pins.package: MSOP-12 and DFN-12, LTC6957-1 and LTC6957-2

pins.name: FILTA
pins.function: CMOS-level control of the input amplifier bandwidth, used with FILTB (Table 1). Referenced to V+.

pins.name: V+
pins.function: Main supply, 3.15 V to 3.45 V. Keep it free of noise and ripple; decouple straight to GND (pin 5) with 0.1 µF.

pins.name: IN+
pins.function: Non-inverting signal input. Differential with IN-, or single-ended with IN- held at a low AC impedance. Takes a sine wave, CML, LVPECL, LVDS, TTL or CMOS. Self-biased near 2 V through internal resistors.

pins.name: IN-
pins.function: Inverting signal input. In single-ended use it needs a capacitor to ground or to the signal's reference.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground. Use a low-inductance ground plane, with a short, direct path to the V+ decoupling capacitor.

pins.name: FILTB
pins.function: Second CMOS-level bandwidth control, used with FILTA (Table 1). If current is forced into this pin, keep its voltage at or below 4 V.

pins.name: SD2
pins.function: CMOS-level shutdown for output 2; high disables it. With SD1 also high the part enters low-power shutdown.

pins.name: OUT2+
pins.function: Output 2, true side. LTC6957-1: LVPECL, terminated with 50 Ω to a rail 2 V below V+. LTC6957-2: LVDS, close to TIA/EIA-644-A.

pins.name: OUT2-
pins.function: Output 2, complement side (LVPECL on the LTC6957-1, LVDS on the LTC6957-2).

pins.name: OUT1-
pins.function: Output 1, complement side (LVPECL on the LTC6957-1, LVDS on the LTC6957-2).

pins.name: OUT1+
pins.function: Output 1, true side. LTC6957-1: LVPECL, terminated with 50 Ω to a rail 2 V below V+. LTC6957-2: LVDS, close to TIA/EIA-644-A.

pins.name: SD1
pins.function: CMOS-level shutdown for output 1; high disables it. With SD2 also high the part enters low-power shutdown.

pins.name: EP
pins.function: DFN exposed pad, ground. Solder it to the board and tie it to GND (pin 5); good thermal contact gives the rated θJA.

notes: Stress above these ratings can damage the part for good; operating at a rating for long periods can shorten its life and reduce its reliability.

Note 2: IN+, IN-, FILTA, FILTB, SD1 and SD2 have steering diodes to both supplies. Driven past either rail, their current is to be held under 10mA. Current forced into FILTB requires pin 6 to stay at or below 4V. For the four logic pins, 10mA is allowed only with the supply at no more than 3.45V; 10mA at the 3.6V absolute-maximum supply can cause voltage-stress damage.

Note 3: At a 3.6V supply the LTC6957-3/LTC6957-4 CMOS outputs survive sinking 30mA while low and sourcing 30mA while high. If an output is overdriven, or kicked past the rails by an inductive load, 30mA can cause damaging voltage stress, and is guaranteed only with VDD at or below 3.15V.

circuits.title: OCXO sine wave to two clock outputs
circuits.description: A 100 MHz, +7 dBm sine wave from an OCXO, terminated in 50 Ω, is AC-coupled into IN+ through 10 nF; IN- is held at AC ground by its own 10 nF. FILTA and FILTB are grounded for full bandwidth, SD1 and SD2 are grounded so both outputs run, and V+ is 3.3 V with a 0.1 µF decoupling capacitor. The two outputs feed PLL chips or system sampling clocks.

circuits.title: Single-ended LVPECL input
circuits.description: One side of an LVPECL driver runs DC-coupled into IN+, with RTERM terminating the line at the receiver. IN- goes to ground through 10 nF. If the termination returns to an actively generated VTT, that capacitor can return to VTT instead of ground for lower noise.

parts.note: line termination, form chosen by the user

circuits.title: Differential LVPECL input
circuits.description: Both sides of an LVPECL driver run DC-coupled into IN+ and IN-. Three equal RTERM resistors in a Y terminate the pair; their common point is a passive VTT. Driving both inputs doubles the differential signal and rejects common-mode noise.

parts.note: 50 Ω for most 3.3 V LVPECL drivers
50 Ω for most 3.3 V LVPECL drivers
50 Ω for most 3.3 V LVPECL drivers

circuits.title: Single-ended 50 Ω source input
circuits.description: A 50 Ω RF source is matched by a 50 Ω shunt resistor and AC-coupled into IN+ through 10 nF; IN- sits at AC ground through 10 nF. A pure tone up to 10 dBm can be applied.

circuits.title: Differential CML input
circuits.description: A CML pair, each line pulled up to the driver's supply by RTERM at the receiver, is AC-coupled through 10 nF capacitors into IN+ and IN-. Coupling capacitors are needed because the CML DC level does not suit the LTC6957 input bias.

circuits.title: Single-ended CML input
circuits.description: One CML line, pulled up by RTERM, is AC-coupled into IN- through 10 nF. Because that signal is referred to the RTERM supply, IN+ is AC-referenced to the same supply through 10 nF. The inputs may be swapped to change polarity.

circuits.title: LVDS input
circuits.description: An LVDS pair is terminated differentially with 110 Ω and AC-coupled through 10 nF capacitors, because the LVDS common-mode level does not suit the LTC6957 input. The termination should match the trace pair's differential impedance (90 Ω to 132 Ω under EIA-644-A) and sit close to the LTC6957. A 3 kΩ resistor across each capacitor makes the link DC-coupled, holding the output polarity with about 100 mV differential when the clock stops.

circuits.title: CMOS input over a 50 Ω trace
circuits.description: A CMOS gate (about 25 Ω output resistance) drives a 75 Ω / 100 Ω divider, which halves its Thevenin voltage and presents 50 Ω to a 50 Ω trace. At the far end the line is AC-coupled into a 50 Ω load across IN+ and IN-, with IN- AC-grounded, halving the swing again: about 800 mVP-P at the input from 3 V CMOS, 1.25 VP-P from 5 V, 600 mVP-P from 2.5 V. The capacitors only block DC and need an impedance well under 50 Ω at the clock frequency; without them the divider draws 12.4 mA from a 3.3 V driver.

parts.note: DC block, impedance well below 50 Ω at the clock frequency
AC coupling, impedance well below 50 Ω at the clock frequency
AC ground for IN-, impedance well below 50 Ω at the clock frequency

notes: The values suit Z0 = 50 Ω and scale for other trace impedances, keeping the Thevenin impedance equal to Z0.

circuits.title: LTC6957-1 LVPECL output termination
circuits.description: The LVPECL output pair runs over 50 Ω traces to the receiver and is terminated there by three 50 Ω resistors in a Y: 100 Ω differential and 75 Ω common mode. The outputs have no internal pull-downs, so this network both terminates and biases them. A capacitor from the Y's midpoint to the return improves common-mode behaviour; a delta of three resistors is an alternative where the common-mode impedance does not matter.

circuits.title: LTC6957-2 LVDS output termination
circuits.description: The LVDS output pair runs over 50 Ω to 60 Ω traces and is terminated across the receiver inputs by 110 Ω.

parts.value: Z0 = 50 Ω to 60 Ω PCB trace

circuits.title: 10 MHz crystal oscillator
circuits.description: An LT1761-3.3 makes the 3.3 V rail from 5 V. The LTC6957-3 is the oscillator's gain stage: OUT1 drives a 10 MHz AT-cut crystal through 100 Ω into IN+, where 150 Ω and 75 pF in series load it to ground; IN- connects to OUT1 through 2 kΩ and to ground through 30 pF. FILTA and FILTB are high for the 50 MHz bandwidth. OUT2 drives a 50 Ω load through 450 Ω, a 0.3 VP-P square wave.

circuits.title: 10 MHz frequency reference input stage with dual CMOS outputs
circuits.description: A 10 MHz reference of -10 dBm to 24 dBm comes in through 0.1 µF to a Coilcraft WBC16-1T transformer whose primary returns to chassis. The centre-tapped secondary, its tap AC-grounded by 0.1 µF, feeds two 100 Ω resistors into a 604 Ω load across which an HSMS-281C anti-parallel Schottky pair sits. Each side is AC-coupled through 0.1 µF into IN+ and IN-. FILTA and FILTB are driven from outside. V+ and VDD each run from 3.3 V with 0.1 µF; SD1, SD2, GND and GNDOUT are grounded. OUT1 and OUT2 give 10 MHz CMOS; OUT2 is also taken through 0.1 µF and a 100 Ω / 100 Ω divider to the phase-noise measurement.

operation.text: Four members share one input stage and differ only in the output: LTC6957-1 LVPECL, LTC6957-2 LVDS, LTC6957-3 CMOS with both outputs in phase, LTC6957-4 CMOS with the two outputs complementary. Each has two outputs. Inputs may be sine waves or logic of any family, at most 2 VP-P, and up to 300 MHz.

The input is a differential NPN pair, protected by diodes against ESD and overdrive, and self-biased through internal resistors (1.2 kΩ from each input to a divider of 1.8 kΩ and 3.2 kΩ, about 64 % of the supply). They are too large to leave an input floating without raising the noise, so both inputs need a low AC impedance; in single-ended use the unused input needs a capacitor to ground or to the signal's reference. The resistors stay connected in shutdown, so shutdown and wake-up do not kick back into the driver and disturb coupling-capacitor charge.

10 nF ceramic capacitors in small SMT cases suit the input networks. Above 100 MHz smaller values may be preferred, to keep away from series resonance, which can add noise even on a capacitor that only grounds the unused input.

FILTA and FILTB set how much bandwidth the first gain stages have (Table 1). Amplifier noise turns into timing noise in inverse proportion to input slew rate, so the best setting depends mainly on slew rate (Table 2) or, for a sine wave, on frequency and amplitude (Table 3). Bandwidth beyond what preserves the input slew rate only adds aliased noise. At 100 MHz the slew rate seen at the input is 628 V/µs at +10 dBm, 198 V/µs at 0 dBm and 63 V/µs at -10 dBm; these call for full bandwidth (both pins low), the 500 MHz setting and the 160 MHz setting in turn. The best and next-best settings are always close, while the worst can be 10 dB noisier. Large, fast inputs gain little from filtering, since the first differential pair limits ahead of the filters.

The delay and skew limits apply to a 100 mV input step overdriving by 50 mV. Less overdrive lengthens tPD and more shortens it; a larger step with the same overdrive lengthens it slightly. With AC coupling, an input duty cycle away from 50 % gives unequal overdrive on rising and falling edges, so the two delays differ and the output duty cycle moves nearer 50 %. The CMOS LTC6957-3/-4 add rising-versus-falling differences of their own (about 120 ps typical), which vary with load, supply, temperature and part; the complementary LTC6957-4 outputs therefore show more skew than the same-direction edges of the LTC6957-3.

Each output is an emitter follower with no internal pull-down, so the load must terminate and bias it: 50 Ω to V+ - 2 V, or a three-resistor Y at the receiver. Shutdown cuts only the current source; the output bases stay tied to their pull-ups, so both outputs go high and the external load still draws current unless disconnected. While entering or leaving shutdown the output levels carry no guarantee; they may settle slowly or give runt pulses, so SD1/SD2 suit slow on/off control, not gating.

The LTC6957-1 needs 3.15 V to 3.45 V between its rails, whatever their absolute levels: ground and 3.3 V, or ECL-style with ground positive, or 2 V and -1.3 V. No supply sequencing is needed. With a 2 V positive rail the terminations go to ground; with the positive rail grounded the outputs survive shorts to ground. FILTA, FILTB, SD1 and SD2 are driven relative to the part's own rails. Since the output biasing depends on the load, supply changes phase-modulate the output; sensitivity is lower when the termination voltage tracks V+ rather than ground.

The outputs meet TIA/EIA-644-A generator requirements except for rise and fall time, which are kept fast; 2.7 pF across the outputs meets the standard. Behaviour in and around shutdown is outside the standard: VOS may settle slowly and runt pulses may appear, so the shutdown pins are for slow power-saving control. The single supply is 3.15 V to 3.45 V; supply noise affects the LVDS version least of all the options.

Capacitive loads are allowed, with rise and fall times growing in proportion beyond a few pF. In shutdown both LTC6957-3 outputs go low; the LTC6957-4 holds OUT1 low and OUT2 high. The outputs cannot go high-impedance, so shutdown cannot multiplex outputs, and around transitions one or two runt pulses can occur. V+ must stay 3.15 V to 3.45 V; VDD may be as low as 2.4 V to drive lower-voltage logic and should not exceed V+ in operation (the part works with VDD a few hundred mV above V+, but load transients use up that margin). With VDD applied before V+, the outputs are high-impedance until V+ passes about 1 V. The four control inputs are referred to V+. Noise or tones on VDD amplitude-modulate the outputs and can become phase noise. Driving capacitance at high frequency raises VDD current well above the no-load dynamic figure.

Every line should be terminated so that each edge arrives at full slew rate; reflections that slow an edge degrade phase noise. Route point to point, not daisy-chained. The CMOS gate driving the LTC6957 is best used for nothing else, or only for the same timing signal, to avoid spurs from other signals in that IC.

A buffer cannot remove phase noise already on its input. A limiter converts any additive disturbance on the clock into phase modulation, so clocks should be routed as sensitive analog signals: away from digital traces and digital power planes, shielded by ground, and not through FPGAs, nor through fan-out chips offering zero delay or adjustable skew. Assume no more than 30 dB to 40 dB of common-mode rejection. A narrow band-pass filter at the inputs removes disturbances far from the carrier; close-in ones must be avoided at the source. Flexible cables can phase-modulate through piezoelectric effects; rigid cable or PCB routing avoids it.

The input stage converts amplitude modulation to phase modulation by less than 0.5°/dB even at 300 MHz. Part of it comes from the low-pass filters, which treat the two sidebands slightly differently near their cutoff; a higher-cutoff filter setting reduces it.

Load disturbances on one output can modulate the other inside the part, for example an FPGA on one output kicking back into an ADC clock on the other. The CMOS versions are the most susceptible. Placing a buffer ahead of the FPGA stops it. On the LVPECL and LVDS versions the supply modulates the outputs very little; on the CMOS versions VDD amplitude-modulates them directly.

Additive phase noise is measured by splitting a filtered 122.88 MHz source into a path through the device and a reference path and comparing them in quadrature on an Agilent E5505/N5500A; the LTC6957-1 runs from 2 V/-1.3 V into a 50 Ω load through a bias tee. Couplers inject and measure a calibration tone 10 kHz from the carrier, and a line stretcher sets quadrature by hand. Of the four versions the LTC6957-1 is the hardest to measure: its wideband noise ties with the CMOS versions for lowest, and its 1/f corner, under 2 kHz, is the lowest of all.
